claims.text: Kioxia's own August 2026 press release is the honest version: it puts **10 million** random-read IOPS at a 512-byte block size in the headline for the GP1 Series, and puts 100 million in a forward-looking clause about “future generations”.

The GP1 is PCIe 6.0, NVMe 2.2, second-generation XL-FLASH, rated up to 50 DWPD — and evaluation samples reach select customers only “by the end of 2026”, explicitly for functional checking, with production specifications subject to change.

Kioxia's April 2026 roadmap page adds the missing detail: the 100 MIOPS figure attaches to a *second-generation* product at a PCIe 7.0 intercept, and the only demonstration of it — 107 MIOPS — ran on an emulation platform, not on silicon.
- {label: "Kioxia — FPGA emulator, 512B", value: 107M, pct: 11}
Micron's 230 million IOPS is the largest published GPU-initiated result and it comes from forty-four Gen6 SSDs behind three Broadcom PCIe switches, scaling linearly from one drive to forty-four.
Divide it out and each drive is contributing roughly 5.2M IOPS — against the 9650's rated 5.5M at *4KB*.
And the schedule risk is structural: PCI-SIG released PCIe 7.0 to members on 11 June 2025, while Gen6 SSDs only entered mass production in 2026 — roughly three years after the Gen6 specification.
Objective Analysis principal Jim Handy — a NAND analyst whose clients are the vendors making the claim — put a public rebuttal under the headline

A 2026 architecture paper from KAIST targeting exactly this roadmap is blunter still: enterprise SSDs support only about 3 MIOPS today, and the benefits of GPU-initiated storage "cannot yet be evaluated because the hardware is not commercially available."
It names no motivating workload at all, and states neither "512 bytes" nor any IOPS figure.

NVIDIA's FMS 2026 announcement blog — the primary document for both SCADA and the cuFile open-sourcing — contains no mention of KV cache, embeddings, vectors, RAG, retrieval, graph analytics or recommenders.
Its measured configuration is the origin of the number: with 512-byte cache lines BaM achieved 85% of peak throughput at 17 MIOPS, against a 4KB configuration that saturated the PCIe link.
| *"Context Memory Caching for Maximizing AI Inferencing"* | KIOXIA CM9 Series | TLC, PCIe 5.0 |

The GP1 press release itself never uses the words "KV cache", "vector", "embedding" or "inference"; its stated purpose is to "extend High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) as a fast flash memory media-based tier".
StorageReview's FMS write-up — the most widely-cited secondary account — asserts that "embeddings run a few hundred bytes, and KV cache blocks are well under a kilobyte."
`2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes` — **320 KiB per token**, across the whole model.

In vLLM's own words, "the new vLLM KV cache layout yields a physical block size of about 0.5-2 MB, while in the old layout it is only a few KB" — and fragmentation, harmless for compute, "is devastating for KV offloading."
llm-d publishes 128-token blocks at roughly 8.6 MB for DeepSeek-R1, and states that Llama-3.1-70B "requires 305 GB of KV-cache for one million tokens"

The Tutti paper measures the pathology directly: reloading a 128K-token KV for a 64-layer model at block size 64 requires fetching roughly 256,000 scattered ~80KB objects, and fixing the layout — not the device — took retrieval from 11.9 GB/s to 25.9 GB/s and cut TTFT 78.3%.
Per-block recompute budgets for a 128-token block run in the low milliseconds, against NVMe access latencies in the hundreds of microseconds — one to two orders of magnitude of headroom.

DeepSeek's Multi-head Latent Attention compresses KV to `(d_c + d_h^R) × l` per token, which for V3's shape is 68.6 KiB — a 57× reduction against multi-head attention, but only about 3.6× against an 8-head GQA baseline at the same depth.
Conventional DRAM contract prices rose approximately 93–98% quarter-on-quarter in 1Q26 alone, lifting DRAM industry revenue 81% QoQ to $97 billion.
TrendForce measures HBM per-wafer revenue as having been *overtaken* by DDR5 64GB RDIMM in 1Q26.

HBM took roughly 22% of top-three DRAM wafer input at end-2026 while producing about 9% of DRAM bits — a real crowding-out mechanism, but one now sustained by multi-year contracts and requalification cost rather than by superior margin.

NAND is not the cheap alternative to a squeezed DRAM market — in 2Q26 NAND contract prices rose 70–75% QoQ, *outpacing* conventional DRAM's 58–63%, and NOR flash and SLC NAND cumulatively more than doubled across the first half of 2026.
Kioxia specifies XL-FLASH at "a read latency of less than 5 microseconds", on a 128Gb SLC die with a 16-plane architecture and a 4KB page.

The first OCP High Bandwidth Flash specification, published on 3 August 2026, defines three bandwidth grades from about 0.4 TB/s to 3.0 TB/s and up to 512GB per stack over a UCIe interface — and states **no latency figure at all**.

A peer-reviewed IEEE Computer Architecture Letters analysis puts flash read energy at 102.4 pJ/bit against HBM3's 4.2 pJ/bit, for a total access path of 110.8 pJ/bit and roughly a 26-fold increase in access energy versus an HBM baseline.

StorageReview instrumented a real KV-offload deployment — four Blackwell GPUs, eight Solidigm D7-PS1030 drives, vLLM plus LMCache — and found the array running at roughly **3.2 drive-writes-per-day against a 3 DWPD rating**, while consuming about one twenty-eighth of available bandwidth.
Scale the measured 0.475 GB/s-per-GPU write rate to a thousand GPUs and you are writing on the order of 15 exabytes a year
Its NVMe-offload configuration costs approximately 4% *more* than the baseline below the crossover, and reaches only 1.5× cost efficiency at 240 concurrent users.

Alibaba and SJTU, at USENIX ATC'25, found that "a KV$ with capacity 2× of the GPU HBM per-GPU is sufficient to approach an ideal hit rate", explicitly "eliminating the cost and complexity of deploying and managing a CPU-RDMA-SSD storage hierarchy."

A 2026 study of coding-agent traces across 43 developers and 4,265 sessions found token-weighted prefix-cache hit rates around 95.8%, with misses clustering exactly at human thinking gaps — and extending eviction from five minutes to one hour raising the hit rate from 85.4% to 98.6% at roughly 2.7× more resident KV.
Buying the first to solve the second is how a memory-tier thesis becomes a write-off — which is what happened the last time, and cost Intel $559 million.

On 5 January 2026, seven months before FMS, NVIDIA announced BlueField-4 and CMX: an Ethernet-attached, RDMA-accessed flash tier inserted into the memory hierarchy as "a new G3.5 layer, an Ethernet-attached flash tier optimized specifically for KV cache", claiming up to 5× tokens per second and 5× power efficiency at petabytes per GPU pod.
Rubin CPX, announced September 2025, is "the first CUDA GPU purpose-built for massive-context AI", and it solves the problem with 128GB of "cost-efficient GDDR7 memory".
As of 10 August 2026 the XIO-SIG GitHub organisation holds a single placeholder repository; the four named projects do not exist.
The shipping cuFile v1.18 documentation still states that every API is issued from the CPU.
Enterprise SSD revenue among the top five suppliers hit $18.46 billion in 1Q26, up 86.1% QoQ, of which roughly 80% was price rather than bits.
SanDisk reported $8.965 billion of FQ4 FY2026 revenue with datacenter at $2.977 billion — roughly a third of the total, up 103% sequentially
